# The book cannot take the test for you {#lesson-retrieval}

This short synthetic lesson demonstrates the writing and EPUB workflow. It is
intentionally shorter than a normal 30-minute study session.

You finish an explanation and everything makes sense. Excellent. Close the book
and explain the main idea. This is where the comfortable nodding often ends.
While you were reading, the explanation was available, supplying connections
you now have to produce yourself. Attempting that reconstruction is retrieval
practice. You may discover a gap even when the original paragraph felt clear.

::: objectives
After this lesson, you can explain how retrieval differs from rereading
(`explain-retrieval`) and construct a simple retrieval task.
:::

## Work through it

Suppose you are learning how to compare two proposed solutions. You read the
criteria, then close the notes and list them from memory. You explain why each
criterion matters before reopening the notes. Your list omits one criterion.
That omission tells you something useful: there is a specific connection to
repair. Check the explanation and try again. Mistakes are useful information
when you follow them with correction, rather than practicing an error unchecked.

Now complete this partly worked example: after reading about a process, close
the book and explain the first two steps. Before reopening it, also explain
____. One useful completion is “why the second step follows from the first.”
That asks for an explanation rather than a memorized label.

For independent practice, choose an idea you recently read. Write one question
that would require you to produce an explanation without the text in view.
Compare your proposed answer to the source, including any important conditions.

## Recap

Reading provides information. Retrieval asks you to produce it. Both belong in
learning; a fluent reading experience alone does not show that you can retrieve
the explanation later. [Research notes](#source-spacing-review) describe the
evidence and its limits.
